segments.title: Advantages of group decisions
segments.script: Involving more people in the decision-making process can greatly improve the quality of a manager's decisions and outcomes. However, involving more people can also increase conflict and generate other challenges. We turn now to the advantages and disadvantages of group decision-making. An advantage to involving groups in decision-making is that you can incorporate different perspectives and ideas. For this advantage to be realized, however, you need a diverse group. In a diverse group, the different group members will each tend to have different preferences, opinions, biases, and stereotypes. Because a variety of viewpoints must be negotiated and worked through, group decision-making creates additional work for a manager, but (provided the group members reflect different perspectives) it also tends to reduce the effects of bias on the outcome. For example, a hiring committee made up of all men might end up hiring a larger proportion of male applicants (simply because they tend to prefer people who are more similar to themselves). But with a hiring committee made up of an equal number of men and women, the bias should be cancelled out, resulting in more applicants being hired based on their qualifications rather than their physical attributes. Having more people involved in decision-making is also beneficial because each individual brings unique information or knowledge to the group, as well as different perspectives on the problem. Additionally, having the participation of multiple people will often lead to more options being generated and to greater intellectual stimulation as group members discuss the available options. Brainstorming is a process of generating as many solutions or options as possible and is a popular technique associated with group decision-making. All of these factors can lead to superior outcomes when groups are involved in decision-making. Furthermore, involving people who will be affected by a decision in the decision-making process will allow those individuals to have a greater understanding of the issues or problems and a greater commitment to the solutions.
keyPoints: Involving more people can improve decisions but also increase conflict and other challenges
A diverse group brings different preferences, opinions, biases and stereotypes, which tends to cancel out individual bias
Each member brings unique information and perspective, which generates more options and more intellectual stimulation
People affected by a decision understand the issues better and commit more to the solution when they helped make it
segments.altExplanation: Groups help decisions in two ways. A mixed group balances out any one person's blind spots, and more people means more facts, more angles, and more ideas on the table. People also buy into a decision more when they had a hand in making it.
segments.deeper: The hiring-committee example shows bias cancelling out only when the group is actually diverse; a group that is uniform in background will not correct for the majority's preferences. This is why the book pairs the case for group decision-making with the later warning that a group's quality depends on how it is formed, not just on there being more people in the room.

checkpoint.prompt: According to the passage, what is brainstorming?
options: Assigning one member to argue against the group
Settling for the first option that is good enough
Generating as many solutions or options as possible
Escalating commitment to an earlier group decision
checkpoint.answer: Generating as many solutions or options as possible
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option defining brainstorming as generating as many solutions or options as possible.

checkpoint.prompt: Explain why group decision-making can be more effective than individual decision-making.
checkpoint.answer: Group decision-making draws on more knowledge and a wider diversity of perspectives than any one person has, and it generates more options through discussion. It also builds greater commitment in the people who took part in making the decision.
checkpoint.rubric: Must mention at least one of: more knowledge or diversity of perspectives, more options generated through discussion, or greater commitment from people who helped make the decision. A bare 'it's better' with no mechanism is not enough.

segments.title: Disadvantages of group decisions
segments.script: Group decision-making is not without challenges. Some groups get bogged down by conflict, while others go to the opposite extreme and push for agreement at the expense of quality discussions. Groupthink occurs when group members choose not to voice their concerns or objections because they would rather keep the peace and not annoy or antagonize others. Sometimes groupthink occurs because the group has a positive team spirit and camaraderie, and individual group members don't want that to change by introducing conflict. It can also occur because past successes have made the team complacent. Often, one individual in the group has more power or exerts more influence than others and discourages those with differing opinions from speaking up (suppression of dissent) to ensure that only their own ideas are implemented. If members of the group are not really contributing their ideas and perspectives, however, then the group is not getting the benefits of group decision-making.
keyPoints: Some groups get bogged down in conflict, others push for agreement at the expense of quality discussion
Groupthink: members hold back concerns or objections to keep the peace and avoid antagonising others
Groupthink can come from a positive team spirit members do not want to disturb, or from complacency after past success
A dominant member can discourage others from speaking up, so the group loses the benefit of multiple perspectives
segments.altExplanation: Two different problems can spoil a group decision. Groupthink is the group agreeing too easily because nobody wants to break the good mood. Suppression of dissent is one strong voice crowding out everyone else's ideas. Either way, the group stops actually using its members' different perspectives.
segments.deeper: Groupthink and suppression of dissent both remove the diversity of viewpoints that section 2.7 says makes group decisions valuable in the first place, just for different reasons: groupthink is a self-imposed silence to preserve harmony, while suppression of dissent is imposed by someone with more power or influence. The book's later section on forming a quality group, with a devil's advocate and encouragement to speak up, responds directly to these two failure modes.

checkpoint.prompt: In the passage, what does suppression of dissent mean?
options: The group settles for the first workable option
A member is assigned to argue against the group's plan
Members avoid conflict to keep the group's mood positive
A powerful member discourages others from voicing differing views
checkpoint.answer: A powerful member discourages others from voicing differing views
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about a more powerful or influential member discouraging others with differing opinions from speaking up.

checkpoint.prompt: What are some things that can prevent groups from making good decisions?
checkpoint.answer: Groups can fail to make good decisions because of groupthink, where members hold back concerns to keep the peace, or because a dominant member suppresses dissent and discourages others from speaking up. Unmanaged conflict can also derail the discussion.
checkpoint.rubric: Must name at least one of: groupthink, suppression of dissent by a dominant or influential member, or excessive/unmanaged conflict, as a reason groups fail to decide well.

segments.title: Forming a quality group
segments.script: Effective managers will try to ensure quality group decision-making by forming groups with diverse members so that a variety of perspectives will contribute to the process. They will also encourage everyone to speak up and voice their opinions and thoughts prior to the group reaching a decision. Sometimes groups will also assign a member to play the devil's advocate in order to reduce groupthink. The devil's advocate intentionally takes on the role of critic. Their job is to point out flawed logic, to challenge the group's evaluations of various alternatives, and to identify weaknesses in proposed solutions. This pushes the other group members to think more deeply about the advantages and disadvantages of proposed solutions before reaching a decision and implementing it. The methods we've just described can all help ensure that groups reach good decisions, but what can a manager do when there is too much conflict within a group? In this situation, managers need to help group members reduce conflict by finding some common ground, areas in which they can agree, such as common interests, values, beliefs, experiences, or goals. Keeping a group focused on a common goal can be a very worthwhile tactic to keep group members working with rather than against one another. Decision-making is a crucial daily activity for managers. Decisions range from small and simple, with straightforward answers, to big and complex, with little clarity about what the best choice will be. Being an effective manager requires learning how to successfully navigate all kinds of decisions. Expertise, which develops gradually through learning and experience, generally improves managerial decision-making, but managers rarely rely solely on their own expertise. They also conduct research and collect information from others; they pay attention to their own biases and to ethical implications; and they think critically about the information that they have received to make decisions that will benefit the organization and its stakeholders.
keyPoints: Effective managers form groups with diverse members and encourage everyone to speak up before a decision is reached
A devil's advocate is assigned to critique the group's logic, evaluations and proposed solutions, reducing groupthink
When conflict runs too high, managers help members find common ground: shared interests, values, beliefs, experiences or goals
Decisions range from small and simple to big and complex; expertise helps, but managers also research, watch their biases, and think critically
segments.altExplanation: A quality group is built, not just assembled: pick diverse members, get everyone talking, and let someone play devil's advocate to stress-test the thinking. When a group gets stuck in conflict, refocusing on shared ground keeps people working with each other instead of against each other. Managers then bring their own research, self-awareness and critical thinking to the final call.
segments.deeper: The devil's advocate role is a deliberate structural fix for groupthink: rather than hoping someone objects naturally, the group assigns the job of objecting to a specific person, which makes dissent expected rather than awkward. Finding common ground addresses conflict without suppressing it, by redirecting the group's attention to interests they already share. The conclusion ties the whole chapter together: expertise, research, awareness of bias, and critical thinking are all inputs, not substitutes, for a manager's judgment.

checkpoint.prompt: When a group has too much conflict, what does the book say managers should help members find?
options: Common ground, such as shared interests, values or goals
A programmed decision rule to skip the discussion
A devil's advocate to intensify the debate
A single dominant voice to settle the disagreement
checkpoint.answer: Common ground, such as shared interests, values or goals
checkpoint.rubric: Must select the option about finding common ground or shared interests, values, beliefs, experiences or goals.

checkpoint.prompt: As a manager, what can you do to enhance the quality of group decision-making?
checkpoint.answer: Managers can form the group with diverse members, encourage everyone to speak up before a decision is made, and assign a devil's advocate to challenge the group's thinking and reduce groupthink. When conflict is high, they can also help members find common ground.
checkpoint.rubric: Must name at least two of: forming a diverse group, encouraging members to speak up, assigning a devil's advocate, or helping members find common ground.
